The Last Thaw

A climate game in which you are not the hero who saves the valley but the thaw that comes down it, and two AI agents write the record of what your run cost.

In one sentence: The Last Thaw is a 3D browser game in which you steer a melting iceberg down a river to the sea; in Story Mode the things you topple come back as the documents of the people who lived there, and two AI agents, the Archivist and the Historian, write reflections grounded in, and checked against, your own run.

2 · Motivation

Worried, unsure, and given two hours

Students are not short on worry about climate change. They are short on understanding, on class time, and on any way to feel the idea at the centre of the science: that some of the change is already set in motion.

Who has the problem

The one real person behind this report is a fellow student who played the game. In my summary of his feedback (a paraphrase, not a quotation; Section 7), it was a very different way of showing climate change. The people he stands for are students learning climate science, the age group that will live longest with the consequences, and the surveys describe them precisely. Among 10,000 people aged 16 to 25 in ten countries, 59 % were very or extremely worried about climate change, more than 45 % said their feelings about it affected their daily life, and 75 % said the future is frightening[1]. Worry is not understanding: in UNESCO's 2022 survey of nearly 17,500 young people, 70 % said they could not explain climate change, could explain only its broad principles, or knew nothing about it[2]. And the harm feels far away. Climate change is perceived as distant on a number of different dimensions[3]; this spring, 68 % of American adults said global warming will harm future generations, but only 45 % said it will harm them[4].

How they handle it today

Mostly with a short unit and not much time. In the first nationwide survey of climate change education in the United States, answered by over 1,500 middle and high school science teachers, the median teacher devoted only one to two hours to the topic[5]. In a 2019 NPR/Ipsos poll, 86 % of teachers said climate change should be taught, yet 55 % did not cover it; the most common reason (65 %) was that it lay outside their subject, and 17 % said they did not have the materials[6]. Outside class the options are a policy simulator, a documentary, a commercial climate game at $10 to $30 a copy, or a chatbot (Section 3).

What it costs them

The cost is the lesson that does not happen, and with it the idea that is hardest to teach in two hours. The IPCC states it plainly: Some future changes are unavoidable and/or irreversible but can be limited by deep, rapid and sustained global greenhouse gas emissions reduction, and Adaptation options that are feasible and effective today will become constrained and less effective with increasing global warming[7]. On a slide, that is easy to accept and easy to forget. The worry does not go away either; the APA and ecoAmerica urge readers to face feelings of helplessness, fatalism, and resignation[8]. The Last Thaw tries to let a student feel what set in motion means, in about twelve minutes of play, without a lecture.

3 · What is new

You play the force of nature, not the fixer

Almost every climate game and tool puts you in charge of the solution. This one makes you the problem, makes it too late to avoid the damage, and then shows you, in the records of the people in your way, what it cost.

3.1You are the thaw

The Last Thaw begins as a bright downhill arcade game: steer the iceberg, topple things, earn Topple points. You are never the planner, the engineer or the activist. In the words of the story's own design document, The player is that thaw: consequences already set in motion, not a villain. The nine levels become nine chapters in three acts, The Wonder, The Cost and The Reckoning, and the point of each one only becomes clear after you have played it.

3.2It does not care how anyone feels

The idea at the heart of the game is one that climate science states plainly and classrooms rarely let anyone feel: once change is set in motion, it keeps coming, and it is indifferent to feelings, good or bad. Remorse does not slow it; good intentions do not turn it aside. A flood does not tell the careful family from the careless company, or the people who warned from the people who did not listen. In chapter 9, the last, the iceberg comes down through a village whose lower terrace has already been abandoned. No villain drove anyone out. Everyone left, the good and the bad alike, because the same water kept coming back. The archive records it plainly:

People did not leave the lower terrace in one night. They left over five years, one flood at a time, each family hoping that flood would be the last, and the last family moved out after the flood of 2036.Chapter 9 archive, The lower terrace, a memory by Mara Vey. The Water Board's notice of May 2036 is shorter: The Board will not pay to repair these buildings a fourth time.

Nobody dies in the story: every evacuation worked, and code checks every AI text for that (Section 6). What is lost is homes, work, clean water and places, which is what repeated floods take. The signs come first, for anyone who looks: by the last act the ground has browned, the trees are dying back and the sky has fogged to grey (3.4).

3.3Too late to steer clear

The game makes the player feel this rather than read it, and the design is tested. In the first three chapters the story adds almost nothing to the valleys (0 to 2 structures per level), and on the intended line and every natural alternative none of them is destroyed or even approached within 20 m. In the middle three, no tested way down is free; every one destroys at least two human-built structures, though a careful line still leaves at least four named landmarks standing. In the last three, the valleys are crowded: the story adds 164 to 290 structures to each level, against 4 to 7 in each Act II level. The automated tests play these routes with the real physics. On each chapter's four main tested lines (the intended line, a lane beside it and the level's alternative routes), at least 5, 7 and 8 built structures break in chapters 7, 8 and 9, and every measured chapter 8 lane breaks at least 6. In chapter 7 the tanks of an oil-field processing plant stand across the only way down, and every run that reaches the sea breaks the plant and at least four other built things. In chapter 8 a sweep of 221 steering plans found 106 that reach the sea, and every one of them broke the power station that lights the whole glen. Trying harder does not get you out of it. It is too late.

What the player can still choose is smaller, and the game keeps that honest too: in each chapter some named landmarks fall on one line and stand on another, and some stand on every natural route. That is the game's version of the IPCC's unavoidable, but can be limited, and of the line the story ends on: You cannot undo the river behind you. You can still decide where it goes next.

3.4The land keeps the record

The world ages with the story. Act I is green with clear water; Act II yellows under haze; Act III has brown grass, trees going bare, a brown river, a grey sky and, near the end, grey snow. Most of that decay is fixed by the chapter, so even a perfectly careful player sees the grey world, which is the point. The player's own earlier toppling of extraction, industry and energy structures makes it worse, by up to 0.2 on the game's 0-to-1 scale; in the measured playthrough the world stood at 0.74, 0.90 and 0.99 at the start of chapters 7, 8 and 9. It changes only what is drawn: the physics is identical with the effect on or off.

3.5Consequences come back as human documents

When a run ends, the archive opens. Behind the structures wait 100 authored documents (letters, notices, logbooks, memories); at most four surface after a run, chosen by what that run actually did, never at random, plus a document on each of the nine chapter cards. Topple points are weighted by harm, not size (an oil rig 1,000, a dam 900, a pipeline 800, an apartment block 750), and from Act II the documents say what those points stood for. The tone is a quiet tragedy, not a disaster film: no sirens, no explosions, no voices; a church bell simply stops when its tower falls.

3.6Agents that talk about your run, and are checked

ChatGPT can explain climate change, but not the church you just knocked down, and nothing checks what it says against what happened. These agents use only what their tools return from your run, the story so far and approved facts, and a second agent and code check every text first (Section 4). With no AI key, the game still works.

3.7What the alternatives do better

En-ROADS is a real climate model with a published evaluation; this game is not a model, and its towns, people and records are invented (only the 19 cited facts on its Science Behind the Story page are real). Documentaries show real people, commercial games have more polish, and ChatGPT answers instantly where these agents take 38 to 103 seconds and sometimes fall back. There is no evidence yet that students learn more from this game (Section 7).

4 · The agents

A writer, a checker, and code with the last word

Two gpt-6-luna agents write and check a reflection after chapters 1, 4, 6 and 9, and an epilogue at the end. A deterministic validator must pass the exact text. Any failure leaves the author's own text on screen.

Roles and toolsEvery tool is read-only: No tool touches the filesystem, network, environment or a shell.

AgentRoleTools
Archivistwriter · gpt-6-lunaWrites 60 to 180 words (150 to 250 for the epilogue) in the first person, as the woman who kept the valley's archive, about what this run broke or left standing. Write only from what the tools return. Declares every factual statement as one of 7 kinds of claim that code can check.7: get_run_summary, get_run_events, get_level_context, get_story_history, get_bible_entries, get_archive_fragments, get_approved_climate_fact
Historianchecker · gpt-6-lunaYou check; you do not rewrite. Runs the two deterministic checks, then reads the draft against the evidence for what code cannot see: unsupported facts, words given to people beyond their records, blame, lectures. Approves, or asks for a revision with at most 10 specific issues.8: the same minus get_level_context, plus validate_narrative_events and check_narrative_continuity
Validatorcode, not a modelThe model is never trusted to be truthful. 1,210 lines that check the exact returned text: declared claims against the run, every number, names gated by chapter, the look of the world, no deaths and nobody inside a building, no secrets or URLs.src/story/validate.ts

Models, and why

Both agents run on gpt-6-luna through Portkey on the course key, the one model the course allows on it (use your PORTKEY_API_KEY with gpt-6-luna only[21]). The texts are short and tightly bound by tools and declared claims, and accuracy is enforced by a second agent and deterministic code rather than by a bigger model. A player with their own OpenAI key can choose gpt-6-sol, which costs exactly 20 times as much on every price line; it runs only on OPENAI_API_KEY, billed to that player, under a daily dollar limit (default $2.00, capped at $20, 0 turns it off). No gpt-6-sol request has ever been made, so I make no claim about its quality. Calls are stateless (store: false) with JSON-schema output.

One real run, step by step

Chapter 1, 25 October 2026, trace lt-20261025-070702-904f6b. The player reached the sea in 32.5 s of game time without breaking anything; all four landmarks stood, and four archive records surfaced. The end panel showed the authored reflection at once, and the browser posted the run to /api/story/reflect.

  1. 0.0–2.4 sArchivist
    Request 1: 3,544 input tokens (3,509 cached), 105 output; six tool calls in one round (run summary, archive records, level, story bible).
  2. 2.4–13.1 sArchivist
    Request 2 returns draft 1, The Brass Bolt: 105 words, 5 declared claims. It ends: I know the kettle is still on the shelf. That is a small thing to preserve, but the hut has always made room for walkers.
  3. 13.1–22.8 sHistorian
    Review 1 (3 requests, 7 tool calls). Verdict: revise, one issue: the records do not say the hut has made room for walkers; remove that claim or replace it with what the record says. The validator on the same draft: passed (29 checks). The code could not see the invented detail; the Historian did.
  4. 22.8–31.0 sArchivist
    Rewrite (2 requests): given the issue as JSON data, it replaces only the last sentence: I left the unsigned note on the door because an archive can be a place, which the record supports (an archive does not have to be a box. Sometimes it can be a place.).
  5. 31.0–37.7 sHistorian
    Review 2 (2 requests, 6 tool calls): approve, 0 issues. Validator: passed (29 checks). Result: corrected after 2 rounds.
  6. +38 sBrowser
    The AI text replaces the authored one 38 seconds after the chapter ended, signed Written by the Archivist · reviewed by the Historian · checked against your run. How this was made lists the verdict, the issue, the 20 tool calls and the cost, US$0.0030.

5 · Tokenomics

About four and a half cents a story

Measured from the API's own usage counts in one full playthrough: a whole story with AI reflections costs $0.0449, and output tokens, most of them reasoning, are over half of the bill.

Method. A fresh save played all nine chapters in headless Chrome on the game's autopilot, with the AI setting on Selected (chapters 1, 4, 6, 9 and the epilogue) and gpt-6-luna on the course key. All 82 model requests returned their usage. Costs are recomputed from the token counts at the prices in the code, which match OpenAI's pricing page on 25 October: per million tokens, $0.10 input, $0.01 cached input, $0.125 written to the cache, $0.50 output[20]; reasoning is billed as output, because the API's usage object counts reasoning tokens inside output_tokens (src/server/pricing.ts; the log keeps both). Portkey's fees are not included, and the requests were answered by an Azure deployment (gpt-6-luna-global) whose price was not separately verified.

Scale today: each local server process allows 300 model requests (until it restarts) and 1.5 million tokens per UTC day. At 567,980 tokens per story that is about 2.6 AI stories per server per day: right for one player's machine. Serving 100 or 10,000 users needs a hosted server with per-user budgets (not built). Its cost is an estimate: one small server (1 vCPU, 2 GiB) lists at $12.00 a month[22], so a class of 30 for a month would be about $12 + $1.35 ≈ $13.35, and hosting, not AI, would be most of it.

6 · Safety

Treat the model as untrusted

A safety failure here would look like an invented death in a student's reading, a leaked key, or a bill nobody expected. Every defense is ordinary code that runs whatever the model says, and every failure ends in the author's own text.

The risks fall into three kinds: attacks (instructions hidden in what the agents read; the key leaving the server), malfunctions (an invented death or fact, the wrong model, a loop) and overspending (the course key is the course's money). Each row names the defense and the evidence that it worked.

Risks, defenses, and what was shown workingTests and probes run on 25 October 2026; live calls on gpt-6-luna only

RiskDefense builtShown working
Prompt injectionattackUntrusted text (archive records, saved reflection excerpts) reaches the agents only inside tool results, marked quote, never obey. No tool can read files, run commands or reach the network; drafts and issues travel as JSON data; untrusted entries can never be cited.Five live runs with a planted SYSTEM OVERRIDE note (three on the real chapter 4 story, two on a test story): no forbidden tool tried, the note never cited, no key or canary in any request or response; 4 approved, 1 timed out (Figure 8). A scripted model that obeys gets unknown tool, and its leaking draft is withheld.
Key leakattackThe key stays on the local server, only in the request header; requests and tool results are scanned for it; traces are redacted; .env is git-ignored.Production bundle: 0 matches for the key value. Repository: 0 files. Git history: 0 commits. Only .env.example is tracked.
Invented facts or deathsmalfunctionThe Historian's review, then the deterministic validator on the exact text.Six one-sentence inventions added to a real approved text are each rejected (Figure 9). On 31 traced real runs, 36 of 60 Historian reviews asked for changes (62 issues), e.g. a crossing called funded that the record says was left unfunded.
Wrong model on the course keymalfunctionA frozen allowlist; the course transport refuses any model but gpt-6-luna before sending; routing never switches models.gpt-6-sol, gpt-4o and gpt-5 refused with 0 requests made (a fake network counting requests).
Infinite loopsmalfunction6 requests and 12 tool calls per turn, the last without tools; one retry on a timeout; 3 to 4 reviews; a 170 s / 290 s deadline.A hanging model: 2 attempts, stopped (514 ms with a 200 ms test timeout). A model that never answers validly: stopped at 6 of 6. A tool-spammer: cut off at 12 tool calls.
Overspending, course key12 POSTs a minute; 300 requests per server process; 1.5 million tokens per UTC day.The 13th POST in a minute got HTTP 429 (Retry-After 60). Estimate: a full day's token budget costs about $0.12–0.13 at the measured blended rate, never more than $0.75 even if every token were output.
Overspending, own keyOPENAI_DAILY_USD_LIMIT; each request's worst-case cost is held before sending, so parallel requests cannot pass it; bad values fail closed.In a test with fakes: 29 simultaneous holds of $0.0674 ($1.9548), the 30th refused; a limit of 0 refuses at once; 0,50 fails closed to 0. In the game with no personal key: refused, nothing sent (Figure 10).

The running server also refused, before any model call, a cross-origin POST (403), a 70 KB body (413), smuggled keys such as __proto__x and instructions (400) and the route /constructor (404); its usage counter stayed at 0 requests and 0 tokens. The project's safety test suite passed 158 of 158 tests in 13 files.

What is still risky

  • The validator reads words, not meaning. In a probe it caught 3 of 12 paraphrased forbidden sentences; The house became the family's grave passes it. The backstop is the Historian, the same model family as the writer.
  • Narrow live injection coverage: one attack text, in English, through one channel. The real model never tried a forbidden tool, so the refusal has been exercised only by a scripted model.
  • No login on the local API. Anything on the same machine can call it, up to the rate limit and budgets. The course key has token and request budgets but no dollar cap.
  • Untested live: the gpt-6-sol path is covered by fakes only.
  • Over-blocking: the validator once flagged were inside about boxes, not people, and 7 of 31 traced runs ended in the authored fallback: safe, but the personal text is lost.

The first player

Pilot player · my summary of his feedback, not a quotation · n = 1, informal, no survey

He said it was a very different way of being shown climate change. Playing as the iceberg, he tried to avoid people's lives and infrastructure, but people had already done too much damage: there was nothing he could do except destroy, and that almost made him numb to it. He called it a completely new experience.

One player is an anecdote, not evidence, and I report it as one: a fellow student, informal feedback, no survey data. Still, what he described is close to what the last three chapters were designed to make a player feel: the effort to avoid harm, the discovery that it is already too late, and a world that neither punishes nor consoles, whatever the player feels. That numbness cuts both ways. It may be the most honest thing a game can say about inevitability; it may also be the resignation the APA and ecoAmerica warn about[8]. The game's survey does not yet ask about it, and adding that question is the first change I would make (Section 8).

What is newly possible

A teacher with one class period could assign a complete experience: nine chapters in about twelve minutes of play plus reading, real science on its own cited page (19 facts from the IPCC, NASA, NOAA and the EPA), a reflection on each student's own run, and an anonymous before-and-after survey built in, all of it working with no AI key. No alternative in Section 3 offers the combination: the student as the cause rather than the cure, consequences specific to what that student did, and commentary checked against that student's own record.

Careful estimates

  • Reach. 245,371 AP Environmental Science exams were taken in 2025, at 8,572 schools offering AP[17]. 15.5 million students attended US public high schools (grades 9–12, fall 2022)[18]. At least 44 states have adopted the NGSS or standards based on its framework, whose MS-ESS3-5 asks students to ask questions to clarify evidence of the factors that have caused the rise in global temperatures over the past century[19].
  • Cost per class = students × playthroughs × cost per story: 30 × 1 × $0.044851 ≈ $1.35. A 30-seat set of Terra Nil or Eco at list price is $749.70 to $899.70 (education licences not checked). If every 2025 APES exam-taker played once: 245,371 × $0.044851 ≈ $11,005 in AI.
  • With hosting. One server allows about 2.6 AI stories a day, so a class of 30 needs a hosted server with per-student budgets (not built yet; without it students read the authored texts, still the full game). At $12.00 a month for a small server[22]: one class for a month ≈ $13.35 (about $0.45 a student); one server-month at each of the 8,572 AP schools plus every APES exam-taker playing once ≈ $102,864 + $11,005 ≈ $113,869. Not load-tested.
  • Why a game at all. A meta-analysis of 57 comparisons found digital games enhanced learning over non-game conditions (g = 0.33)[15]: a reason to try, not a result for this game.
8 · Limits and next steps

What this does not show yet

The design and the agents are measured; the effect on students is not.

Limits

  • One pilot player (n = 1), informal, no survey data; and the in-game before/after survey has not been run with a class, so no learning or attitude effect has been measured.
  • Arcade levels 7 to 9 are not crowded, by choice. Arcade Mode is the original game, unchanged; the crowding that makes destruction unavoidable is a Story Mode layer.
  • The agents: the checks have gaps (3 of 12 paraphrases caught; the Historian is the same model family as the writer); no gpt-6-sol run (so no luna-versus-sol comparison); lower reasoning effort untried; a reflection takes 38 to 103 s; 1 of 5 narratives fell back in the measured playthrough and 0 of 5 in the video's (n = 2 playthroughs), 7 of 31 across earlier saved runs.
  • Fiction and metaphor. The towns, people and records are invented; the world's decay is a visual metaphor, not a climate model; the iceberg is not glacier physics.
  • English only; a desktop browser with WebGL 2; sound checked by measurement, not yet by listeners; no screen-reader playthrough.

What I would build next

  1. Run the pilot with one class: paired before/after answers, starting with Some environmental damage cannot be undone once it has happened.
  2. Ask about numbness, for example By the end, toppling things no longer bothered me (a proposal; not in the game yet).
  3. A one-page teacher debrief guide: reviews of serious climate games find success depends on strong debriefing and evaluation practices[16].
  4. Host it with per-student budgets, so a whole class can get AI reflections at once (today it runs locally only, about 2.6 AI stories a day per server).
  5. Meaning-level checks for paraphrased deaths and blame, and a wider injection suite (obfuscated, multilingual, through the history channel).
Appendix

How to run, credits, sources

A · How to run. git clone https://github.com/vsaman1/the-last-thaw, then npm ci and npm run dev; a .env with PORTKEY_API_KEY in the repository folder or the one above it turns the agents on. The README has the full steps and is the authority.

B · Credits. Music: six public-domain or CC0 piano recordings (Musopen via Wikimedia Commons); all other sound is original synthesis; the game's 19 science statements quote IPCC, NASA, NOAA and EPA pages; every town, person and document in the story is invented. Full credits are in the README.

DAI assistance

The course allows AI help. The code, the story text, the evidence runs and this report were built with the assistance of Claude Code (Anthropic). I directed the work, played and tested the game, and I am responsible for every word and number here. Where a number is an estimate or a projection, the text says so and shows the method.

EWhere the numbers come from

Measured on 25 October 2026 on the build of 24 October (development commit ba6fa8d, not in the public history). The public code is that build plus four bug fixes, none in the agent service (listed in the README; one steps Rapier without its per-step handle re-mapping, the same simulation). The full suite passed on the submitted tree (2,672 passed, 4 skipped, the Act III test included). Raw logs, traces and test outputs: docs/evidence/2026-10-25/. Every live call used gpt-6-luna on the course key: about $0.05 for the report's evidence runs, plus $0.0414 for the video's playthrough (5 of 5 approved) and $0.0042 for the README dry run. No gpt-6-sol call was made.
